Title: The Sun Never Set (Part 9 of 10): The Fall Begins, 1939–1959

Summary: The Second World War broke the empire's power in Asia. Singapore fell in 1942, the Bengal famine of 1943 killed millions, and within three years of victory Britain had left India, Pakistan, Burma, Ceylon and Palestine. Yet in the 1950s it fought hard to hold on elsewhere, in Malaya, Kenya, Cyprus, British Guiana and at Suez. This post covers 1939 to 1959, a period of both rapid withdrawal and some of the empire's most violent counter-insurgency campaigns.

---

## The big picture

In 1939 Britain still ruled about a quarter of the world. The empire again went to war as a block, though this time the dominions declared war separately, and Ireland stayed neutral. India was declared at war by the Viceroy without consulting any Indian leader, which led Congress's provincial governments to resign.

The empire's contribution was enormous again. The Indian Army grew to about 2.5 million men, the largest volunteer army in history. But the war also exposed British weakness. Japan's rapid conquest of Hong Kong, Malaya, Singapore and Burma in 1941–1942 destroyed the myth of British invincibility in Asia.

After 1945 a nearly bankrupt Britain, dependent on American loans, gave up its largest possessions quickly. Partition in South Asia and the end of the Palestine mandate were both chaotic and deadly. In other places, especially where there were white settlers, strategic bases or valuable resources, Britain fought to stay.

## Main timeline: the Second World War (1939–1945)

| Date | What happened | Where |
|---|---|---|
| September 1939 | Britain declares war (3 September); the Viceroy declares war for India | Global |
| October 1939 | Congress ministries resign in protest | India |
| March 1940 | **Lahore Resolution** of the Muslim League calls for independent Muslim-majority states | India |
| May–June 1940 | Churchill becomes Prime Minister; Dunkirk evacuation; fall of France | Europe |
| April–May 1941 | **Anglo-Iraqi War** against Rashid Ali's pro-Axis government | Iraq |
| August 1941 | Anglo-Soviet invasion of Iran; **Atlantic Charter** | Iran. Churchill said the Charter's self-determination clause did not apply to the British Empire |
| December 1941 | Japan attacks Malaya, Pearl Harbor and **Hong Kong** (Hong Kong falls on 25 December) | Asia |
| 15 February 1942 | **Fall of Singapore**; about 80,000 to 85,000 British, Indian and Australian troops surrender | Singapore. Churchill called it the "worst disaster" in British military history |
| February 1942 | Abdeen Palace incident: British tanks force King Farouk to appoint a pro-British government | Egypt |
| March–May 1942 | Japan takes Burma; hundreds of thousands of Indian refugees flee on foot | Burma |
| March–April 1942 | Cripps Mission offers dominion status after the war; rejected | India |
| August 1942 | **Quit India Movement**; Congress leadership arrested | India |
| October–November 1942 | El Alamein | Egypt |
| 1943 | **Bengal Famine** | Bengal. About three million die |
| October 1943 | Subhas Chandra Bose forms the Provisional Government of Free India and leads the **Indian National Army** with Japan | Southeast Asia |
| March–July 1944 | **Imphal and Kohima** | Northeast India; the turning point in Burma |
| 1944 | Universal adult suffrage in Jamaica | Jamaica |
| May 1945 | Rangoon retaken; war in Europe ends | Burma and Europe |
| July 1945 | Labour wins the general election | Britain |
| August 1945 | Atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki; Japan surrenders | Japan |
| October 1945 | UN Charter in force; Pan-African Congress in Manchester (Nkrumah and Kenyatta attend) | Global and Britain |

## Main timeline: withdrawal and counter-insurgency (1945–1959)

| Date | What happened | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| November 1945 | INA trials at the Red Fort | Huge popular support for the accused |
| February 1946 | **Royal Indian Navy mutiny** in Bombay and other ports | Shows Britain can no longer rely on Indian forces |
| July 1946 | Irgun bombs the **King David Hotel** in Jerusalem; 91 killed | Palestine |
| August 1946 | Direct Action Day and the Great Calcutta Killings | Thousands die in communal violence |
| 1946 | Malayan Union imposed, then replaced by the Federation (1948) after Malay protest | |
| 15 August 1947 | **Independence and Partition of India and Pakistan** | Around 15 million displaced; deaths estimated from about 200,000 to 2 million |
| October 1947 | First Indo-Pakistani War over Kashmir | |
| January 1948 | Burma independent (outside the Commonwealth); Gandhi assassinated (30 January) | |
| February 1948 | Ceylon independent; Accra riots in the Gold Coast | |
| May 1948 | **End of the Palestine Mandate (14 May)**; State of Israel declared; the Nakba | Around 700,000 Palestinians flee or are expelled |
| June 1948 | *Empire Windrush* reaches Tilbury; **Malayan Emergency** declared | The Emergency lasts until 1960 |
| 1948 | British Nationality Act creates "Citizen of the United Kingdom and Colonies" | |
| April 1949 | Ireland becomes a republic and leaves the Commonwealth; **London Declaration** allows republics such as India to stay in the Commonwealth | The modern Commonwealth begins |
| 1948–1951 | Batang Kali massacre (December 1948); Briggs Plan resettles about 500,000 Chinese Malayans in "New Villages" | Malaya |
| 1951 | Iran nationalises the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company | |
| 1951 | Nkrumah's Convention People's Party wins elections in the Gold Coast | |
| 1952 | Egyptian Revolution (July); **Kenya Emergency** declared (October) | |
| 1953 | **Coup in Iran** (August), organised by the CIA and MI6; British Guiana's elected government removed after 133 days (October); Central African Federation formed | |
| 1953 | Coronation of Elizabeth II | |
| 1954 | Anglo-Egyptian agreement to withdraw from the Canal Zone | |
| April 1955 | **EOKA campaign** begins in Cyprus | |
| 1956 | Sudan independent (1 January); **Suez Crisis** (October–November) | US pressure forces Britain and France to withdraw; widely seen as the end of Britain as an independent great power |
| March 1957 | **Ghana** independent | First sub-Saharan African colony to gain independence |
| August 1957 | **Malaya** independent | |
| 1957–1959 | Jebel Akhdar War in Oman, with British SAS involvement | |
| 1958 | West Indies Federation formed; Notting Hill riots; Iraq's monarchy overthrown | |
| March 1959 | **Hola massacre** in Kenya: 11 detainees beaten to death; **Nyasaland Emergency** | The Devlin Report calls Nyasaland "a police state" |
| 1959 | Singapore self-governing; Cyprus independence agreed | |

## Resistance: risings and counter-insurgencies

| Years | Who | Where | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1942–1944 | Quit India Movement | India | Over 100,000 arrested; around 1,000 or more killed (figures disputed) |
| 1943–1945 | Indian National Army | Burma and Northeast India | Defeated militarily, but the trials helped end British rule |
| 1944–1948 | Jewish insurgency (Irgun, Lehi, Haganah at times) | Palestine | Britain hands the problem to the UN |
| 1946 | Royal Indian Navy mutiny | Bombay, Karachi and elsewhere | Ended within days |
| 1946–1951 | Tebhaga and Telangana movements | Bengal and Hyderabad | Peasant risings |
| 1948–1960 | Malayan Communist Party (Malayan National Liberation Army) | Malaya | Defeated |
| 1948 | Accra riots | Gold Coast | Speed up reform |
| 1952–1960 | **Mau Mau (Kenya Land and Freedom Army)** | Kenya | Defeated; over 11,000 rebels killed, over 1,000 hanged, tens of thousands detained in camps |
| 1953 | People's Progressive Party (Cheddi Jagan) | British Guiana | Elected government removed |
| 1955–1959 | EOKA | Cyprus | Independence in 1960, but not union with Greece |
| 1956 | Egypt under Nasser | Suez Canal | Britain forced to withdraw |
| 1959 | Nyasaland African Congress | Nyasaland | State of emergency; Hastings Banda jailed |

## Things that happened at the same time

- **February 1942.** The fall of Singapore and the Abdeen Palace incident in Egypt happened within two weeks. Britain was losing face in Asia while openly overruling a nominally independent government in Egypt.
- **1943.** The Bengal famine was at its peak while Bose's Indian National Army was being formed and the war in Europe was turning in the Allies' favour.
- **1947–1948.** In about nine months, Britain left India, Pakistan, Burma, Ceylon and Palestine. In the same weeks of mid-1948, it declared the Malayan Emergency and the *Windrush* docked at Tilbury.
- **1952–1953.** The Kenya Emergency, the Iran coup, the removal of British Guiana's elected government and the coronation of Elizabeth II happened within twelve months.
- **Autumn 1956.** The Suez invasion and the Soviet crushing of the Hungarian Revolution happened in the same weeks. US anger at Britain over Suez was increased by the fact that it distracted from Hungary.
- **March 1957.** Ghana became independent in the same month as the Treaty of Rome; Britain was not yet a member of the European project it would later join.

## Sources and flags

- Christopher Bayly and Tim Harper, *Forgotten Armies* (2004) and *Forgotten Wars* (2007), on Britain's Asian empire 1941–1957.
- Yasmin Khan, *The Great Partition* (2007) and *The Raj at War* (2015).
- Madhusree Mukerjee, *Churchill's Secret War* (2010), and Amartya Sen, *Poverty and Famines* (1981), on Bengal 1943.
- Caroline Elkins, *Imperial Reckoning* (2005) and *Legacy of Violence* (2022); David Anderson, *Histories of the Hanged* (2005), on Kenya.
- Huw Bennett, *Fighting the Mau Mau* (2013).
- The UK National Archives "migrated archives" (FCO 141), released after the Mau Mau case: https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk
- **Flag:** Partition death estimates range widely (about 200,000 to 2 million) and there is no consensus. The Bengal famine is usually put at about 3 million deaths, though some estimates are lower or higher. Mau Mau figures: the official British count of rebels killed was over 11,000; Elkins's estimate of total Kikuyu deaths is much higher and is disputed by other historians, especially David Anderson and some demographers. The causes of the Bengal famine, and how much responsibility lies with British wartime decisions, are debated.
